infact.justification: The claim is refuted because election laws vary by state and do not mandate that all ballots must arrive on or before Election Day to be counted. Many states allow for a grace period where mail-in ballots are considered valid if they are [postmarked by Election Day](https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2020/politics/mail-in-voting/) but arrive later. For example, the Supreme Court upheld rules in [Pennsylvania](https://www.npr.org/2020/10/19/922411176/supreme-court-rules-pennsylvania-can-count-ballots-received-after-election-day) that allow officials to count absentee ballots received as late as the Friday after Election Day, provided they have a timely postmark, and [North Carolina](https://www.npr.org/2020/10/19/922411176/supreme-court-rules-pennsylvania-can-count-ballots-received-after-election-day) has similarly allowed ballots to arrive as late as November 12 under certain conditions. Additionally, [Texas](https://www.sos.state.tx.us/elections/laws/advisory2020-20.shtml) provides specific provisions for counting late-arriving ballots from military and overseas voters.
